passage: People ask what I, Madhav, actually do in meetings. Mostly I listen. Last month Shankar pitched a plan to our team: a new delivery route for the bakery's orders. It was gorgeous. Step one, the new van arrives by the 5th. Step two, the two drivers finish training in a week. Step three, the café chain signs by the 15th. Step four, our order software syncs with their system. Everyone nodded, me too at first. Then I counted. Four steps, and every one had to land on time. I said, "Each of these is fairly likely on its own. All four together? A lot less." Shankar looked annoyed for a second, then laughed and said we'd plan a backup for the van. It wasn't about shooting him down. It was just counting.

qa.q: What was Shankar's plan for?
qa.a: A new delivery route for the bakery's orders.

qa.q: What made Madhav stop nodding along?
qa.a: Madhav counted the steps and realised that four steps all landing on time was much less likely than any single one, which made the lovely pitch feel shakier.

qa.q: What did the team do after Madhav spoke, and why does it help?
qa.a: They planned a backup for the van, so the whole plan doesn't collapse if that one step slips.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when Madhav raised the point?
qa.a: Shankar looked annoyed for a second, likely feeling the pitch was being picked apart, but then laughed and accepted the backup idea.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing a detailed pitch and reminding the team that four steps together are less likely than any one.

passage: I sat next to Jahnavi at Thursday's planning meeting, so I saw it up close. Rafiq was presenting our NGO's library drive for village schools: publishers donate two thousand books by August, the district office approves transport, forty college volunteers sign up, and every school has a reading corner running by Children's Day. His slides were lovely, full of photos and dates. People clapped. Jahnavi didn't. She was quietly writing numbers beside each step; I only noticed because she tilted her notebook toward me. Then she raised her hand. "This is a strong plan. But it needs all four things to happen. If each is fairly likely, all four together are much less likely. Which step can we make not depend on the others?" Rafiq paused, then nodded slowly. I can't say what she was thinking, but she didn't look smug. She looked careful.

qa.a: She was quietly writing numbers beside each step.

qa.a: It suggests she liked the plan but felt cautious, because she was working out how likely it was for all four steps to happen together.

Monday. Tushar pitched his idea for the team outing: rent a bus, reach the hill fort by nine, cook lunch at the rest house, watch the sunset from the top, be back by ten. He told it so vividly that everyone was sold. Omkar listened, arms folded, and said nothing yet.
Wednesday. Omkar caught Tushar by the coffee machine. "I love it. But the bus, the ghat road, the rest-house booking, the weather, twenty people being on time... each one is probably fine. All of them together is a lot to ask." Tushar grumbled but agreed to drop the rest-house lunch and pack food instead.
Saturday. The bus came forty minutes late. The rest house, it turned out, had closed for repairs. The team ate packed parathas on the fort wall and still made the sunset. On the ride back, Tushar sat down next to Omkar and said, "Fine. You were right about the lunch."

qa.a: It had closed for repairs.

qa.q: Why might Omkar have waited until Wednesday to say something?
qa.a: Omkar may not have wanted to deflate the group's excitement in the meeting, and a quiet word by the coffee machine would feel less like a public challenge to Tushar.

qa.q: Which change to the plan saved the day, and why?
qa.a: Dropping the rest-house lunch and packing food removed one step that had to go right, so the closed rest house didn't ruin the trip.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Omkar's advice after Saturday?
qa.a: Tushar now sees it as helpful rather than spoiling the fun, which is why he admitted Omkar was right about the lunch.

Zainab, come, sit. You asked how to speak up in a meeting without sounding negative. Let me tell you about my first year at the export house in Tiruppur.
The sales head pitched a plan for a new buyer in Spain. It was beautiful. The cotton arrives by the tenth, the dye house finishes in a week, the embroidery unit takes the rush order, the ship sails on the twenty-eighth, the buyer approves the samples at once. Everyone clapped.
I was twenty-five, the only woman at that table, and scared, but I said it anyway. "Every step sounds likely. But all five have to go right together. Even if each is quite likely, together it's much less." I suggested one spare week and a backup dye house.
Nobody clapped for me. But the dye house did break down that month, and the spare week saved the order. That is how Rehana learned to count steps, beta.

qa.q: When was the ship due to sail in the sales head's plan?
qa.a: On the twenty-eighth.

qa.q: What was young Rehana feeling when she spoke up, and what made her do it anyway?
qa.a: She was scared, as a twenty-five-year-old in her first year, but she saw that five steps all had to go right together and felt the team needed to hear it.

qa.q: Which choice made Rehana's warning useful rather than just negative?
qa.a: She paired the warning with fixes, one spare week and a backup dye house, so the team had a way forward when the dye house broke down.

qa.q: Why might the others in the meeting have clapped for the pitch but not for Rehana?
qa.a: The detailed pitch made success feel vivid and exciting, while Rehana's point felt like cold water, even though it protected the order.

"So the council approves the permit next week," Sumit said, pacing the community-hall floor. "Then the factory funds the nets, two hundred volunteers come every Sunday, the schools join by August, and by Diwali the lake has ducks again."
"Ducks," someone whispered happily.
Charu put down her tea. "Sumit, I love it. Can I ask something annoying?"
"You always do."
"Every step you said has an 'and' after it. Permit and funding and two hundred people and schools. What if the factory says no?"
"It won't. It's all connected."
"That's what worries me. Connected means if one piece fails, the rest wait. What's the one step we can do without anyone's permission?"
Sumit stopped pacing. "Cleaning the east bank ourselves."
"Then let's start there this Sunday."

passage: I still think about the Tuesday Kamal pitched the new booking feature. I'm Elizabeth, the quiet tester on a team of nine in Leeds, and I usually keep my head down. Everyone was nodding. I was nodding too, and at the same time counting on my fingers under the table. Four things, all needing to go right, each one resting on the last. I said so, as kindly as I could. Kamal looked annoyed for a second, then drew four boxes on the whiteboard and asked which one was shakiest. The hotels, it turned out. We rang two of them first.

Planning meeting, 12 March. My notes as project coordinator.
Salma pitched the new rural delivery scheme today. It was the most convincing pitch I've heard all year: drones from the district hub, village volunteers to receive them, a mobile app in three languages, a state subsidy by June, and a partnership with the postal department. The room loved it. People were nodding at every step.
I felt the pull too. Then I noticed: every step depended on the one before. I asked the team, gently, "If each of these five things has a good chance, say seven in ten, what's the chance all five happen?" Someone did it on a phone. Less than two in ten. Salma looked stung, then thoughtful.
Next step: we'll pilot just the volunteer network in one village first. Naveen

Wednesday night.
Francis gave the pitch today for the new customer-loyalty plan. It was brilliant, honestly. Personal messages, a points app, a partnership with the gym next door, a TV ad, and a festival launch. By the end, half the room was clapping.
I clapped too. But on the train home I kept thinking. Every single thing had to work. The app on time. The gym saying yes. The TV slot. The festival date. If any one failed, the story fell apart. The more detailed it got, the more believable it felt, and the less likely it was.
Tomorrow I'll ask Francis, kindly, if we can list each step with a rough chance next to it. And maybe start with the one part that doesn't depend on anyone else, the personal messages.
Thomas

The dairy cooperative's meeting room in Moga smelled of chai and fresh paint. Gurpreet stood by the chart paper, glowing.
"Step one, we get the state grant. Step two, the cheese machine arrives from Pune by March. Step three, the hotel in Chandigarh signs for weekly orders. Step four, the members agree to extra milk collection at night. Step five, we're making a profit by Diwali."

The Friday pitch in the Copenhagen office ran on Oskar's slides and Oskar's energy.
"A big creator shares it in week one," he said, clicking. "That brings fifty thousand downloads, twenty percent subscribe, and the investor we met in Berlin sees the numbers and doubles our funding by summer."
The room was nodding. The numbers were so specific they felt like facts.
Bilal, two seats from the end, drew a small chain on his notepad: share, downloads, subscribe, investor, funding. Five links.
When questions opened, he said, "I love the energy. One thought: each step depends on the one before. If the share doesn't happen, or only ten percent subscribe, the rest doesn't follow. Could we plan for each link breaking?"
Oskar paused, then laughed. "You're ruining my movie."
"I just want the sequel," Bilal said. The team leader wrote BACKUP PER STEP on the whiteboard.

Subject: Thoughts on yesterday's rollout pitch
Hi Manjula,
Before we sign, one small worry about the vendor's pitch. It was brilliant: approval from the state portal in week two, all 40 branches trained by week four, the old system switched off in week five, fully live in six weeks, and zero downtime. Everyone in the room was nodding, me included.
But when I wrote it out, it's really five separate things that each have to go right, in order. Even if each one is quite likely, the chance of all five working together is a lot lower than any one of them. The detail made it feel more certain, when it actually makes it less so.
Could we ask them for a plan B for the two riskiest steps, and a date range instead of one date?
Thanks,
Indu
